newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala military police rebel over severance.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala military police rebel over severance.

text.p: One general remained a virtual hostage on Saturday night inside the fortified compound of Guatemala military police, who are demanding guarantees of severance pay when peacetime claims their jobs.

"I'm not sure yet," General Hugo Aguilar of the presidential honour guard told Reuters when asked whether he was free to leave. Aguilar said he knew the 400 military police would say "no" if he asked them for permission to leave.
Hundreds of disgruntled military police in their fourth day of revolt roamed around the compound with assault rifles but heeded their commanders' orders to respect superior officers.

Earlier in the day, military police shoved and threatened two other generals who came to the compound with Aguilar to tell them the government needed time to come up with a concrete offer of severance pay.

Despite his delicate position as a negotiating pawn, Aguilar said he would willingly stay the night to help bring a peaceful conclusion to the first show of military discontent with terms of a December peace treaty ending 36 years of civil war.

The military police seized their own compound on Wednesday night, saying they were uncertain of their future when the goverment dissolves their 4,000-person army unit to fulfil promises contained in the peace accords.
Peace accords were being implemented after decades of civil war. An estimated 140,000 people were either killed or listed as missing during the conflict.
The army, which will be reduced by one third this year, has played a pivotal, and at times brutal, role in political life for much of Guatemala's recent history.
The government has minimised the revolt so far. Presidential spokesman Ricardo de la Torre has labeled the uprising a "labor dispute," not an act of rebellion.
"What's happening is that because of apprehension about their future some of them have acted a little violent, but it's not a rebellion," Aguilar said.
Military police have refused to report to work guarding banks and businesses in the capital during the protest.

Their sympathetic commander, Col. Leonel de Leon, addressed them on Saturday night and told them to return to normal work and to form a 12-15 person negotiating team to work out a deal with the government.

Police complain the guerrillas of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit had won a better deal in the peace accords than they did. International aid will provide job training and housing assistance for ex-rebels.
